4963: The assessee was a dealer of the business of the assessee in the year 1958 and the income of the company was assessed to tax under section 40(1)(a) of the Act. The Income Tax Officer held that the income from the business was not assessable to tax as it had been assessed under section 257 of the Act and that the assessee was liable to pay tax under the Act. In appeal to this Court, HELD: 1. Section 4(1) of the Act, which is relevant for our present purpose reads thus: "4(1) Where any person has been assessed to income-tax under section 107, or has been assessed, he shall be deemed to have been assessed in the assessment year in which the income is chargeable to tax at the rate specified in the Schedule, or has escaped assessment for the assessment years 1956-57 and 1956-57; Provided that where the income has been determined by the Income-tax Officer under section 158, or has not been assessed by the assessee, the income shall be computed in accordance with the provisions of this Chapter.
5994: The appellant was appointed as a Director of the Indian Medical College in the State of Bihar. He was appointed to the post of Assistant Engineer on the basis of his appointment as a Member of the Central Administrative Tribunal. The appellant filed an application before the Tribunal for grant of leave to appeal against the order of the Tribunal and the Tribunal by its order dated 9.8.1988. The Tribunal allowed the application holding that the respondent had been appointed as Assistant Engineer, Grade I and he was not eligible for consideration under the provisions of the [Punjab Civil Services (Classification, Control and Appeal) Rules, 1968] and the Rules framed thereunder. The Tribunal held that the appellant was not entitled to any relief. The Tribunal dismissed the application of the appellant on the ground that the Tribunal had no jurisdiction to entertain the application filed by the appellant under Section 11(6) of the Act and that the High Court had no power to interfere with the order passed by the Tribunal on the grounds that the order was not made by the Tribunal. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The High Court has rightly held that there is no scope for interference by this Court.
7130: The appellant was a tenant of the property in dispute and was a tenant. The appellant filed a suit for eviction on the ground that he had been in possession of the premises in dispute. The trial court decreed the suit holding that the appellant was not a tenant within the meaning of section 4(1)(a) of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882 (hereinafter referred to as 'the Act') and that the suit was barred by limitation. The High Court dismissed the suit. The appellant preferred an appeal before the High Court. The High Court, however, allowed the appeal and set aside the judgment of the trial court. The High Court's judgment is challenged in this appeal. The appellant has come up in appeal before us by special leave. The question which arises for consideration in this appeal is whether the appellant is a tenant under the [Bombay Rent Control Act, 1957] (hereinafter, "the Act") or not. Section 4 of the Act provides that where any person is a landlord of a building or a building which is a building under the provisions of the Act, the tenant shall be deemed to have become a tenant if he is a member of the family of the landlord.
6118: The appellant was employed as a workman of the factory at the relevant time and was working as a clerk in the State of Uttar Pradesh. The appellant had been employed as an employee of the Corporation on the basis of the recommendations made by the Central Government under section 4(1) of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947. The appellant filed a writ petition before the High Court of Madhya Pradesh challenging the validity of the order of termination dated March 31, 1985. The High Court dismissed the writ petition. The High Court, however, held that the appellant was not entitled to any relief. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The appellant is a workman. He has been employed in the factory for the purpose of the establishment of the factory. [58C-D] 2. The appellant has been engaged in the business of manufacturing and selling and selling the same to the factory and is engaged in such business. It is not necessary to go into the question whether the appellant is an employer. The appellant cannot be said to have been employed by the appellant as a worker of the appellant. [59F-G] 3. The appellant does not dispute that he is a casual labourer and is not a workman; he is not an employee but is a permanent workman.
4860: The appellant was convicted under section 302 read with section 149 I.P.C. and sentenced to imprisonment for life and a fine of Rs. 500/- in default to suffer rigorous imprisonment for one year. The High Court dismissed the appeal filed by the State against the order of acquittal passed by the trial court. The High Court, however, confirmed the conviction and sentence awarded by the Trial Court. The High court held that the evidence of PW-1 was not sufficient to convict the appellant. Allowing the appeal, HELD: 1. The High Court's judgment is based on the evidence adduced by the prosecution and the evidence led by the prosecution. The High Courts have not considered the evidence on record but have found that the prosecution has failed to prove its case beyond reasonable doubt. [576F] 2. The High court's view that the conviction of the appellant under section 141 I.P. C., was not justified, is unsustainable. [589B] 3. The High court, therefore, committed an error of law in holding that the appellant had been guilty of the offence under section 324 I.PC. The High Court. was not justified in interfering with the order passed by this Court.
660: The appellant was a tenant of the appellant's house in the year 1952. He was a member of the Hindu undivided family and was a partner in the said house. The appellant claimed that he had been a partner of the deceased and his wife and that he was a resident of the same village. The appellant contended that the appellant was not a partner but as a partner and that the respondent was a partner. The appellant also contended that he could not be a partner at the time of the death of the deceased. The appellant denied that he is a partner or a partner who is a member thereof. The appellant contested the claim of the appellant on the ground that the deceased was a partnership firm and that it was a firm and not a firm. The High Court held that the evidence of the witnesses was not sufficient to prove that the husband was a member, and that there was no evidence to show that the wife was a partners and that she was a director of the family. The High Court, however, held that there were no evidence on record to show how the appellant could have been held to be a member and that if the appellant had been held a partner then the appellant would have been entitled to the benefit of section 14(1)(a), (b) and (c) of the Act.
3436: The appellant was a dealer in the goods and was a manufacturer of the goods for the purpose of manufacturing the goods. The appellant had purchased the goods from the respondent on the basis of the price of the imported goods and the sale proceeds were paid by the respondent. The respondent filed an application under section 66(1) of the Act before the Sales Tax Appellate Tribunal, Madras Bench, which was allowed by the High Court holding that the goods were not liable to be taxed at the rate of Rs. 5,000/- per annum and that the sales tax authorities had no jurisdiction to levy excise duty on the goods manufactured by the appellant. The High Court held that the levy of excise duty, as it stood at the relevant time, was not a tax on the sale or purchase of the goods, but was a tax upon the sale of the goods. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (i) The levy of duty on goods manufactured or produced by the appellant is a tax and is not a tax. [657 D] (ii) The levy is not an excise duty.
6276: The appellants were the owners of the lands in question and were the tenants of the appellants. They were the respondents in the writ petitions filed by them before the High Court of Gujarat at Ahmedabad challenging the validity of the impugned notification dated April 30, 1980. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the Act was not a special law for the purpose of the Act, and that the provisions of the Act were ultra vires the Constitution. Allowing the appeals, HELD: 1. The Act is a special statute and is a general statute. It is a statutory provision which can be made for the protection of the interests of the general public. [57B] 2. The Act does not provide for the compulsory acquisition of land for the benefit of the public or for any other purpose. The Act provides for the imposition of a tax on the land in question. The Act has been enacted to provide for a special procedure for the acquisition of land. The Act also provides for a general procedure for taking action for the enforcement of the Act. The Act itself provides for an appeal from the decision of the appropriate authority to the State Government under the Act.
2727: The appellant was a Hindu undivided family of the appellant. He was a member of the Hindu undivided family. The appellant filed an application under section 14(1)(a) of the Act for the grant of a decree for partition and separate possession of the property in question. The trial court dismissed the application. The High Court held that the appellant had no right to be a Hindu joint family property. The High Court, however, allowed the appeal and set aside the order of the trial court. The appellant preferred an appeal to this Court. The High Court's judgment was affirmed by the High Court. The appellant contended that the deed of gift was not a Hindu law and therefore the appellant could not have been a Hindu widow of the respondent. The High court held that there was no question of the appellant being a Hindu or a Hindu law; it was not necessary for the appellant to prove that the property was a joint family property within the meaning of section 14(1) (b) of the Act. The High Court. HELD: 1. The High Courts are not concerned with the question whether the appellant is a Hindu Hindu undivided family, but whether he is a member or a member thereof. [576A] 2. The High court, therefore, was not justified in holding that the document was a genuine document.
3356: The appellant was convicted under section 302 read with section 34 of the Indian Penal Code and sentenced to imprisonment for life and a fine of Rs. 500/- in default to suffer rigorous imprisonment for one year and a further fine of Rs.500/-. The High Court dismissed the appeal filed by the State against the order of conviction and sentence. The High Court, however, upheld the conviction and sentence of the appellant. The High court has confirmed the conviction of the appellant under section 323 I.P.C. and sentenced him to undergo rigorous imprisonment of two years and to pay a fine thereof. The High Court's judgment is challenged before us by the appellant in this appeal. The appellant is a resident of village Kamalpur and is a partner of the firm of M/s. Ramesh Chandra and Mst. Ram and Md. Ram are partners of the firm. The firm is a partnership firm and the firm is the wife of the firm, and the partnership firm is also a partnership firm. The partnership firm was dissolved on the basis of the partnership deed dated 21.7.1951. The partnership deed was executed on 22.9.1952. The partnership was dissolved by the firm on the ground that the partnership was not dissolved on account of the business of the partnership.
1531: The assessee was a partner of the firm and was a partner. The assessee filed an application under section 24B of the Income Tax Act, 1961 for the assessment year 1950-51. The assessee claimed that the income of the assessee was not liable to be taxed in the hands of the assessee. The High Court held that the assessee had no right to claim the benefit of the said provision. The High Court, however, held that there was no question of law as to the meaning of the expression "income of any other person" in the Act. The High Court's view was that the assessee's income was not assessable to tax under the Act and the income was liable to tax only on the ground that it was not chargeable to tax. The High court also held that since the assessee did not have any interest in the business of the assessee, the income could not be assessed as income of that person and the assessee could not claim exemption from the income under section 14(1). The High Court. HELD: (1) The High Courts are not concerned with the interpretation of the words "income derived by the assessee from any other person.
2609: The Government of Andhra Pradesh issued a notification under section 3 of the Act on March 31, 1966 declaring that the Government of India was not a public servant and that the said notification was not in accordance with the provisions of the Act. The Government issued a Notification dated April 1, 1966 under section 4 of the Act, which provided that the State Government may by notification in the Official Gazette, declare that the notification dated May 30, 1966 is ultra vires the Constitution and further that it is not necessary to make any provision for the exercise of the power conferred by section 3 or section 3A of the Act." The notification was published in the Gazette on February 28, 1966. The notification under Section 4 of Act No. XVI of 1966 was published on March 29, 1966. It was published as per the notification under [section 4] of the Act: "No person shall be entitled to any compensation for his land or any part thereof except with the previous sanction of the Central Government. The Government may, by notification specify the grounds on which the notification has been issued, and the grounds upon which the declaration is based. The Government may at any time call for the report from the Government and take such action as it thinks fit.
1522: The appellant was convicted under section 302 I.P.C. and sentenced to imprisonment for life and a fine of Rs. 500/- in default to suffer rigorous imprisonment for one year and to pay a fine thereof. The High Court held that the appellant had failed to prove that he had been acquitted by the trial court and that he was not guilty of the offence under section 147 I.P. C., and that the conviction of the appellant under section 323 I.PC. was not justified. Held, that the High Court was right in holding that the evidence of the prosecution witnesses was not sufficient to sustain the conviction and sentence of the appellant. [579B-D] JUDGMENT: CRIMINAL APPELLATE JURISDICTION: Criminal Appeal No. 435 of 1968. Appeal from the judgment and order dated September 7, 1968 of the Allahabad High Court in Criminal Revision No. 648 of 1967. S. N. Andley, J. B. Dadachanji, O. C. Mathur and Ravinder Narain, for the appellants. M. K. Ramamurthy, R. H. Dhebar, S. N. Mukherjee, for the respondent.
2392: The appellant was a member of the Legislative Assembly and was elected as a citizen of India on November 1, 1963. He was elected by the State Government in exercise of its powers under section 163-A of the Criminal Procedure Code. The appellant filed an application for leave to appeal to this Court under section 482 of the Code of Criminal Procedure. The High Court dismissed the petition holding that the appellant had been guilty of contempt of court and that he was not a citizen within the meaning of section 143 of the Cr.P.C. The High Court, however, held that the order of dismissal was not vitiated by any error of law or that it was not maintainable. Allowing the appeal, HELD: 1. The High Court's judgment is based on the principle that if the appellant is a citizen and has been convicted of contempt for the offence of contempt under section 302 IPC, the High Court will have to consider whether the conviction of the appellant should be set aside. [751C] 2. The High Courts are not concerned with the question whether the appellant was guilty of the offences punishable under section 498-A IPC but whether the sentence imposed upon him was a punishment for the offence.
1378: The appellant was convicted under section 302 I.P.C. and sentenced to imprisonment for life and a fine of Rs. 500/- in default to suffer rigorous imprisonment for one year. The High Court held that the conviction of the appellant was not justified. The High Court, however, confirmed the conviction and sentence of the appellant. The appellant has been acquitted by the High Court. The High court dismissed the appeal filed by the State against the order of acquittal passed by the Sessions Judge. The High Court's judgment is challenged before us by the appellant in this appeal. The appellant is a resident of village Khurshid at the Police Station. He is a member of the Scheduled Caste and is a citizen of India. He is an Indian citizen. His wife is a foreigner and he is a public servant of the State. The appellant who is a Government servant of a State, is a government servant, and his family is a private person. The appellant had no right to be prosecuted for having committed an offence punishable under section 149 I.P. C., and he was also a public servant. The prosecution case is that on the date of the incident the appellant came to the house of the respondent and started abusing him and assaulted him.
4071: The appellant was a tenant of the appellant. The respondent filed an application under section 123 of the Code of Civil Procedure for eviction of the appellant on the ground that he had not been in occupation of the premises in question. The trial court dismissed the application. The High Court held that the order of eviction was not vitiated by any error of law or that the appellant was not a tenant within the meaning of section 123(1) of the Act. The High Court, however, allowed the appeal and set aside the order dated April 20, 1966 and directed the appellant to pay the arrears of rent to the respondent. The appellant preferred an appeal before the High Court. The High Court's judgment was challenged by the appellant before this Court. The learned counsel for the appellant contended that the High Court was wrong in holding that the decree passed by the trial court was invalid. The High court held that there was no evidence to show that the respondent had been in possession of the premises. The High court, therefore, held that it was not necessary to go into the question whether the appellant could be said to have been in possession.
3168: The appellant company was a public limited company incorporated under the Companies Act, 1956. The appellant was a company incorporated in the year 1962. The appellant had been carrying on business of manufacturing and selling and selling goods for the purpose of manufacturing or selling goods. The appellant carried on business as a public company under the provisions of the Companies Act. The appellant filed an application under section 138 of the Act praying that the order of the High Court be set aside and the matter be remanded to the trial court for fresh disposal in accordance with law. The appellant contended that the High Court, while allowing the appeal of the appellant held that the appellant was not a public company. The High Court dismissed the appeal. Allowing the appeal, HELD: 1. The appellant is a public company, which is a company registered under the Societies Registration Act, 1860. [768B] 2. The facts are that the respondent company was engaged in the business of selling and sale of goods and it was engaged by the appellant in the manufacture of goods for sale of goods. The respondent company had been engaged in manufacturing and sale and purchase of goods from the appellant. The appellant did not carry on any trade or business. The appellant claimed that he was a private company and was not liable to pay sales tax under the Act.
232: The appellant was a public limited company incorporated under the Indian Companies Act, 1913, and was a company incorporated in the State of Mysore. The appellant filed an application for winding up of the company under section 34, Indian Companies Act No. 29 of 1950. The appellant claimed that he had been a public company incorporated within the meaning of section 2(d)(i) of the Companies Act, 1956 and that he was a private limited company constituted under the Companies Act. The appellant contended that the appellant was not a public company, but was a 'public company' within the definition of "public company" as defined in section 2(f) of the Banking Regulation Act, 1944. The appellant contends that the High Court was right in holding that the provisions of section 302 of the Indian Contract Act were applicable to the facts of the present case. The appellant has also relied on the decision of this Court in [Commissioner of Income-tax, Bombay v. M/s. [Hoecha Mills Co. Ltd.] [1964] 1 S.C.R. 587. (2) [1966] 3 S.CR. 792. (3) [1961] 1 S. C. R. 593. (4) [1960] 1 L.L.J. 23].
4568: The appellants were appointed as Assistant Professor in the Central Health Service and were appointed to the post of Professor in a University called the "Medical College" for the purpose of the Central Public Service Commission. The High Court held that the appointment of the appellant was not an appointment under the Central Government Service. The High Court, however, did not consider it necessary to decide the question whether the appointment made by the appellant is valid or not. [98C-D] (2) The High Court's decision on the question of the applicability of article 227 of the Constitution to the appointment to the posts of Professor of Medicine and the post to which the appellant belonged, was erroneous. The High court held that there was no provision for the appointment and the appointment was not valid. [988B] (3) The High Courts have not considered the question as to whether the order of the High Court was vitiated by mala fides or illegal. [986G-H; 983A] (4) The High Court. was not justified in holding that the order passed by the High Court, though it was not challenged before the High Court. The High court, therefore, was right in holding the appellants' case that the High Court-had jurisdiction to entertain the writ petition.
2440: The appellant company was engaged in the business of manufacturing and selling and selling the products of the appellant. The appellant company, a company incorporated under the Companies Act, 1956 (hereinafter referred to as "the Act") was engaged by the appellant company for the purpose of carrying on its business. The appellant Company claimed that the appellant Company had been engaged in manufacturing and sale of the products manufactured by it from its factory at the relevant time and that the said goods were not being used for the manufacture of the same or similar goods in the factory of the appellant company. The appellant filed an application before the tribunal for the issue of a writ of mandamus directing the appellant to pay the amount of wages to the workmen of the respondent. The tribunal allowed the claim of the respondent company and directed the appellant company, to pay to the appellant the sum of Rs. 1,00,000/- which was paid to the appellant, and directed that the amount be paid to them within three months from the date of the order. The appellant preferred an appeal to the tribunal which was dismissed by the tribunal on the ground that the award of the tribunal was not binding on the appellant Company. The tribunal held that the Tribunal was right in holding that the reference made by the Tribunal to the Tribunal did not affect the validity of the award.
2913: The assessee was a partner in the business of the assessee firm and the income from the business was assessed to tax under section 14(1) of the Indian Income Tax Act, 1922. The High Court held that the income of the company was not liable to be taxed as it was not a case of income from business. The High Court, however, held that there was no evidence on record to show that the assessee had been carrying on business in the name of the assessee's firm. The High court also held that since the assessee was not an assessee in the assessment proceedings before the Income-tax Officer the assessee could not be said to have been taxed in the hands of the assessee. The High Court's judgment is based on the decision of this Court in [Commissioner of Income-tax, Bombay v. G.C. Agrawal], [1964] 1 S.C.R. 587. In that case, the assessee claimed that the amount of Rs. 4,682/-, which was the income for the year ending 31st March, 1958 was not assessable to tax. The High Court. HELD: 1. The High Courts are right in holding that the sum of Rs. 1,982/- was not chargeable to tax at the rate of Rs. 78,693/-.
1697: The appellant was a dealer under the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922 and was a registered dealer under an Indian Income-tax Act of 1919. The appellant claimed exemption from tax under section 25(4) of the Act on the ground that it had not been paid tax under the Act. The High Court held that the appellant was entitled to exemption from tax. The High Court, however, held that there was no provision in the Act for the assessment year 1951-52, and the appellant could not be assessed as a dealer in the assessment year. The High court held that it was not necessary to consider the question whether the appellant is liable to pay tax under Section 25(4). The High Court's judgment was affirmed by the High Court. Allowing the appeal, HELD: 1. The High Courts have taken the view that the provisions of the [Income Tax Act] are applicable to the facts of this case. The appellant has not been able to show that he had received the tax under any other law. [42F-G] 2. The High Court. of Madras v. M/s. [1947] A.C. 691, referred to. 3. The High court's decision in the case of Commissioner of Income-tax, Bombay v. Mst. Ramachandran & Co. Ltd., [1961] 1 S.C.R.
3844: The appellant was a Hindu undivided family of the deceased and his wife was the sole owner of the properties in dispute. The appellant filed an application under section 14(1)(a) of the Indian Succession Act, 1922 (hereinafter referred to as 'the Act') for eviction of the appellant from the properties of the appellant. The trial court held that the appellant had been in possession of the property by virtue of the provisions of the Act and that he was entitled to the benefit of the Act. The trial court, however, held that there was no evidence on record to show that the respondent had been married to the appellant and that the marriage between him and the appellant was not a joint family property. The trial Court held that it was not necessary for the appellant to prove that the suit property was the joint family property of the respondent. The High Court also held that since the appellant did not have any interest in the property, the appellant could not be said to have been in possession. The High Court, therefore, set aside the order of the trial court. The appellant preferred an appeal to this Court. The High court dismissed the appeal. The appellant then filed a revision petition before the High Court which was allowed by the impugned judgment and order dated April 20, 1966. The High Court's judgment is challenged in this appeal.
5364: The appellant was appointed as a member of the Corporation on the basis of the recommendations made by the Board of Directors of the Corporation. The appellant filed an application under Article 226 of the Constitution before the High Court of Judicature at Allahabad for quashing the order of termination of his service and for quashment of his services in terms of the provisions of the Act. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the order passed by the High Court, which was challenged by the appellant in this appeal by special leave has been violated by the appellant. The appellant is a retired employee of the appellant who is a member and is a member. He is a workman within the meaning of Article 12 of the Constitution. [689B] JUDGMENT: CIVIL APPELLATE JURISDICTION: Civil Appeal No. 4749 of 1988. From the Judgment and Order dated 21.12.1985 of the Delhi High Court in Writ Petition No. 5375 of 1987. V.P.S. Pathak, S.K. Sharma, K.G. Balakrishnan, M.C. Chagla and B.N. Srivastava, for the Appellant. S.V. Gupte, K.R. Garg, S.P. Singh, Ms. A. Subhashini and R.K.
3542: The appellant was a member of the Indian Administrative Service and was appointed as a Public Service Commission in the year 1975. He was confirmed in the post of Assistant Engineer on the basis of his appointment as a Superintendent of Police in the State of Punjab and was posted as a Special Public Service Commission. The respondent filed an application under section 19(1)(b) of the Act for grant of leave to appeal against the judgment of the Single Judge of the High Court in the writ petition before the Division Bench of the Punjab & Haryana High Court. The Division Bench by its order dated 1 st April, 1976 allowed the petition holding that the respondent was not a Public Servant. The Division Bench, however, held that the order of the learned Single Judge was not sustainable in law. Allowing the appeal, HELD: 1. The respondent was a Public Service; he was not entitled to any relief. [59D-E] 2. The respondent had been appointed as an Additional District Judge, Bhiwani, but he was appointed only as a Civil Judge and not as a Judicial Officer. The respondent did not have any right to be considered for promotion to the post in question. The respondent could not have been appointed to the posts in question.
266: The appellant company was a company incorporated under the Companies Act, 1956. The appellant company, which is a company registered under the Indian Companies Act and its members were registered as an association of persons under the provisions of the [Companies Act] and its members. The appellant Company was a public limited company incorporated in the Companies Act. The appellant firm was a private limited company constituted under the [Societies Registration Act, 1860]. The appellant filed a petition under article 226 of the Constitution before the High Court of Judicature at Bombay praying for a writ of mandamus directing the appellant to pay the amount of Rs. 1,00,000/- to the appellant. The appellant contended that the order passed by the High court was not a valid order and that the appellant had no jurisdiction to make any further proceedings under section 5(2) of the Act. The High Court dismissed the petition. Allowing the appeal, HELD: (1) The appellant was a party to the proceedings under the Act and the High Court, therefore, was right in holding that the provisions contained in section 5(1) of the Act were not applicable to the facts of the present case. [579B-C] (2) The High Court, on the other hand, held that the Act did not apply to the case of the appellant company.
3210: The appellant company was a company incorporated under the Companies Act, 1956. The appellant company, in its registered office at New Delhi was a public limited company incorporated in the year 1962. The appellant Company was a private limited company and it was a commercial establishment under the [Bombay Municipal Corporation Act, 1956]. The appellant firm was a corporation registered under the Bombay Municipal Corporation, Bombay and was registered as a public sector undertaking under the provisions of the [Maharashtra Municipal Corporation Act] (hereinafter referred to as 'the Act'). The appellant filed an application for registration of the said business under section 4(1)(b) of the Act on the ground that the said trade is not a public purpose within the meaning of section 2(5) of the Act. The appellant contended that the appellant company had been a public utility establishment, and therefore, the appellant was not a private sector undertaking. The appellant contends that the respondent company was not an industrial concern within the definition of "public purpose" under section 2(6) of the Act, and that the appellant's case was that the company was an industrial establishment within the scope of the definition clause in section 2(7) of the Act; that the respondent-company was also a public charitable institution within the ambit of section 4(1) of the Act: that the business of the company is a public purpose.
1974: The appellant was a partner of the firm in the year 1958 and was a partner. The assessee filed an application under section 66A of the Income-tax Act, 1922 for the assessment years 1958-58, 1960-67, 1961-62 and 1962-63 on the ground that the income of the company was not liable to tax under section 4(1)(d). The Appellate Assistant Commissioner held that the Income Tax Officer had no jurisdiction to assess the income from the business of the firm. The Appellate Tribunal held that there was no evidence to show that the assessee was a partnership firm and that the amount of income was liable to tax. The Appellate Tribunal, however, held that it was not a partnership firm, but a partnership firm. The High Court held that as the assessee had not been a partner in the firm and the income was not chargeable to tax at the time of the assessment. The High Court, therefore, set aside the order of the Appellate Assistant Commissioner. The High court held that since the assessee did not have any liability to tax the income which was liable to, tax, the High Court was right in holding that the question whether the income could be assessed to tax was not one of fact or of law.
6003: The appellant was appointed as Assistant Engineer in the State of Uttar Pradesh on the basis of a certificate issued by the High Court under Article 226 of the Constitution of India for appointment to the post of Deputy Secretary to the Government of India. The appellant filed an application before the High Court, which was dismissed by the impugned judgment and order dated 30th April, 1983. The High Court allowed the writ petition holding that the appellant was not entitled to any relief against the order of the High Court. Allowing the appeal by special leave, HELD: 1. The appellant is a public limited company incorporated under the Companies Act, 1956 and is a private limited company. It is a company incorporated in the Companies Act and is engaged in the business of manufacturing and selling and selling the products of the Company. The appellant has been carrying on business of manufacture and sale of goods and services rendered by it to its members and also to its members. [109H-109A] 2. The appellant had been working as Assistant Director of the Company in the year 1964 and he was working as a Director of M/s. Shyam Sunder Pawar and M/s Shyam Lal Choudhary and Mst. Shyam Lal, who were working as Additional Chief Secretary to Government, the appellant had no right to claim any relief.
5141: The appellant was a dealer of the appellant's factory in the State of Uttar Pradesh and was a manufacturer of the said factory. The appellant claimed that he had been a dealer under the provisions of the Act and the Rules framed thereunder. The appellant contended that the levy of duty on the basis of the licence fee was not a tax on the ground that it was a tax which was leviable under the Act. The High Court held that the appellant was not liable to pay duty as a dealer but only a dealer who was a dealer. The High Court, however, held that there was no provision for payment of duty and the appellant could not be taxed at all. Allowing the appeal, HELD: 1. The appellant is a dealer in the manufacture of goods and is a manufacturer, and the same is a sale of goods by the manufacturer and is not a dealer within the meaning of section 2(1)(d). [798F-G] 2. The appellant has not been a dealer/dealer in any of the goods and the sales of the goods. The appellant cannot be said to have been a manufacturer.
2207: The appellant was a dealer of the goods in question and was a registered dealer under the Bombay Sales Tax Act, 1956. The respondent filed an application for a certificate to appeal to this Court on the ground that the sales tax had been paid by the appellant on the basis of the sale price of the goods. The High Court allowed the petition holding that the amount of tax payable by the respondent was not a revenue receipt. The High Court, however, held that the appellant was not liable to pay any amount as it was a revenue receipt and therefore the appellant could not be said to have been a dealer under section 2(1)(a) of the Act. The High court dismissed the appeal. Allowing the appeal, HELD: 1. The High Court's view is that the transaction in question must be deemed to have taken place within the meaning of section 2(1) of the Act and not within the definition of "dealer" under section 2 (1)(a). [68A-B] 2. The High Courts are not concerned with the interpretation of section 5(2) of the Act, but only with regard to the interpretation placed upon them by the High Court. [69D-E].
2593: The appellant was a public servant, and the appellant was appointed as a Government servant of the State of Gujarat under section 10(3) of the Act on the ground that he had been appointed as an Assistant Director in the State and was not a Government servant. The appellant filed a suit against the appellant for recovery of arrears of salary and other allowances from the date of his appointment as a Director of the State. The trial court dismissed the suit. The appellant preferred an appeal to the High Court which was allowed by the impugned judgment and order dated February 22, 1963. The High Court held that the appellant had no jurisdiction to entertain the suit and the appeal was barred by limitation. Allowing the appeal, HELD: 1. The appellant is entitled to the relief claimed in the suit as a public servant under section 10 of the Act. [68D] 2. The appellant has no right to claim any relief. [69G-H; 69A-B] 3. The appellant cannot be said to have been appointed a Director in respect of the period of his appointment. He could not be appointed as Director of a Government servant; he could not claim any relief under section 11 of the Act, but he could only be appointed a Director.
1195: The appellant was a lessee of the land in question and was a tenant of the appellant. The appellant filed an application under section 3(1) of the Act for eviction of the appellant on the ground that he had been a lessee, but the appellant did not have any right to be evicted from the land. The appellant contended that the appellant was not a lessee. The appellant contends that the lease was a lease and the appellant could not be evicted. The appellant urged that the respondent was a sub-lessee and the lease deed was executed by the appellant in favour of the respondent. The appellant denied the allegation that the leasehold rights were created by the Government of India and that the grant was made by the State of Bihar in favour of' the State. The appellant also contended that there was no valid lease and therefore the appellant should be deemed to be a lessee; that the lessee was a lessor and that he was entitled to the benefit of section 2(1)(a) of the Act. The High Court held that the appellant's case was not one of fact and the High Court was not justified in holding that the tenancy was a lease-deed.
1406: The appellant was employed as a workman in the factory of the appellant and was employed by him as a clerk in the factory. The appellant had been working as a Clerk in that factory and he was not entitled to any relief. The appellant contended that the appellant was not a workman. The appellant did not raise any objection to the maintainability of the application under article 226 of the Constitution. Held, that the Tribunal was right in holding that the order of dismissal was not binding on the appellant because it was not an order made by the High Court under article 136. The appellant could not have raised this contention before the Tribunal. The only question which arises for consideration is whether the order passed by the Tribunal is binding on him. The appellant has no right to claim any relief under section 33 of the Act. The appeal is accordingly allowed with costs. Appeal dismissed. (1) [1962] 1 S.C.R. 834. PETITIONER: THE STATE OF MAHARASHTRA Vs. RESPONDENT: M/S. BALAKRISHNA & ORS. DATE OF JUDGMENT: 11/10/1961 BENCH: SHAH, J.C. BENKATARAMIAH, E.S.
2627: The appellant was a tenant of the premises in question on the ground that he had no right to claim any interest in the property and that the appellant had no right, title or interest in it and that he was entitled to recover the rent from the respondent. The High Court held that the respondent was not entitled to the benefit of section 115 of the Act as it stood at the relevant time and that there was no provision for the payment of rent by the respondent to the appellant. The High Court, however, held that since the appellant was not a tenant under the Act, the appellant could not be said to have been in possession of the suit property. The High court further held that it was not necessary for the appellant to prove that the premises were let out to him by the respondents. The High Court's judgment was affirmed by the High Court. The High court, therefore, set aside the order of the Trial Court and remanded the matter to the High Court for fresh consideration by the trial court. The High Courts have come to the conclusion that the order passed by the Trial, being an order made by the District Judge under section 11 of the Act, is not sustainable in law. The High Court. has come up for final hearing before us. The appeal is allowed with costs throughout. Appeal allowed.
6270: The appellant was appointed as a Assistant Engineer in the State of Uttar Pradesh on the basis of the recommendation made by the Central Administrative Tribunal, New Delhi. The appellant filed an application under Article 226 of the Constitution before the High Court of Judicature at Allahabad praying for a writ of mandamus directing the respondent to appoint a person as Assistant Engineer, to be appointed as Assistant Teacher in terms of the provisions of the Act and the Rules framed thereunder. The High Court allowed the writ petition and quashed the order of the Tribunal holding that the appellant was not a member of the Union Territory of Delhi and he was entitled to be considered for appointment as Assistant Teachers in the Central Civil Services (Classification, Control and Appeal) Rules, 1961. The High Court, however, dismissed the writ petition. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The appellant is a citizen of India and is a resident of the State and is not a citizen within the meaning of Article 12 of the Constitution. [579B] 2. The appellant has been appointed as an Assistant Engineer. He is a member and is also a member thereof. He is not an employee of the State. The appellant cannot be said to have been appointed in accordance with the rules framed under the Act.
3924: The appellant was a woman aged about 25 years and was married to one R.K. Bansal, the wife of the deceased. The appellant had been living with her husband in the house of the deceased and his wife was living with her. The appellant did not have any other family members but he was not in a position to make any statement that she was a child of the appellant. [468G-H] (2) The appellant could not be convicted under Section 302 read with Section 34 IPC as he was a minor at the time of the incident. [479F-G] (3) The conviction of the appellant under Section 323 I.P.C. is based on circumstantial evidence. The appellant has been acquitted by the trial court and the High Court has confirmed the conviction of him under Section 342, I.P. C., and sentenced him to undergo rigorous imprisonment for three years. The appellant is before us in this appeal. The appellant will be entitled to the benefit of doubt. [477A-D] JUDGMENT: CRIMINAL APPELLATE JURISDICTION: Criminal Appeal No. 536 of 1971. From the Judgment and Order dated 21.12.1973 of the Andhra Pradesh High Court in Crl. Misc.
6778: The appellant was a public servant of the State of Uttar Pradesh and was a member of the Scheduled Caste and was an employee of the Union of India. The appellant filed a writ petition in the High Court of Madhya Pradesh, which was dismissed by the impugned judgment dated 27.8.1978. The High Court allowed the writ petition holding that the appellant was not a public servant, as he had been a member thereof and that the order of dismissal passed by the High Court, was illegal and without jurisdiction. The High Court, however, held that the High Court's power under Article 226 of the Constitution to issue a writ of mandamus or any other appropriate writ, direction or order directing the appellant to pay the amount of compensation to the appellant. The High court also held that there was no question of the appellant being a public servant' within the meaning of Section 2(1)(a) of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947. The High Court-dismissed the appeal on the ground that the appeal was not maintainable because the appellant had not been a public servants within the definition of "public servant" under Section 2(1) of the Act. The High Courts upheld the order passed by learned Single Judge and dismissed the appeal. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD.
2124: The appellant was a member of the Scheduled Caste and was a resident of the State of Madhya Pradesh. He was a member. The appellant filed an application under section 10(2) of the Representation of the People Act, 1951 for the recovery of the amount due to him from the appellant. The appellant claimed that he had been dispossessed by the appellant from the State Government and that he was not a member thereof. The appellant contended that he could not be held to be a member in the Legislative Assembly of the State. The appellant contested the election petition on the ground that he did not possess the requisite qualifications prescribed by the Act and that the appellant was not entitled to the benefit of the Act. Held, that the provisions of the Act were applicable to the facts of the present case. The appellant had no right to claim the benefit under the Act as it was not liable to be taxed at all. The appellant could not have been convicted under section 120-B of the Indian Penal Code and section 13(1)(d) of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947. The appellant was, therefore, entitled to be set at liberty if he had not been given any opportunity to defend himself.
78: The appellant was a tenant of the premises in question under the provisions of the Bombay Rent Control Act, 1950. The appellant filed an application for eviction of the appellant on the ground that he had no right to recover the arrears of rent from the tenant. The High Court dismissed the application. The appellant preferred an appeal to this Court. The High Court, however, held that the appellant was not a tenant within the meaning of section 2(a), (b) and (c) of the Act and therefore the appellant could not be evicted from the premises. The High Court's judgment was affirmed by the High Court. Allowing the appeal, HELD: 1. The appellant is a tenant under the Bombay Tenancy Act, 1950, and is a landlord under the Act. [89A-B] 2. Section 3 of the said Act provides that where any person has been or is a member of a family of which he is a member, the tenant shall be deemed to have become a tenant if he is not a member thereof. The provision of section 3 of that Act is not applicable to the present case. [810F] 3. The appellant cannot be evicted. He must be a tenant in respect of the property in question. The tenant must be deemed as a tenant and not as a member thereof and not otherwise.
4316: The appellant was a workman of the appellant. He was employed as an industrial company in the State of Andhra Pradesh. The appellant filed a writ petition before the High Court of Andhra Pradesh challenging the order of the Tribunal and the High Court. The High Court dismissed the writ petition. The High Court, by its judgment dated 18th February, 1970, allowed the writ petition and set aside the award of the Tribunal. The appellant preferred an appeal to this Court under Article 136 of the Constitution of India for quashing the award. The appellant challenged the validity of the award on the ground that it violated the provisions of the Act and the Rules framed thereunder. The High court held that the award was not made within the period of limitation prescribed under the Act. The High Court's view was that the reference to the Industrial Tribunal was not maintainable because the appellant had not been given any opportunity to show cause against the award and that the appellant was entitled to be paid wages under the award as it was not a workman. The High court, however, held that there was no question of the appellant being entitled to the benefit of the Award and the appellant could not have been given the benefit under the Award. Allowing the appeal, HELD.
1778: The appellant company was a workman in the State of Bombay and its employees were employed by the appellant as an industrial dispute under the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947. The appellant filed a suit for declaration that the contract of employment was not a contract of employment. The appellant contended that the agreement was not an agreement between the parties and that the appellant had no right to claim any benefit under the contract. The appellant also contended that there was no agreement between him and the appellant and the respondent and that he was entitled to claim the benefit of the agreement on the ground that the contractor was not one of the workmen. The appellant contested the suit on the grounds that the terms of the contract were not binding on the appellant and, therefore, the appellant was not entitled to the benefit under section 11(2)(vi). The appellant then contended that it was not necessary to go into the question whether the contract was a contract or not and therefore the appellant could not be held to have been a party to the dispute. Held, that the provisions of the Act are not applicable to the facts of this case. The appellant is a workman. He has not been able to show that he had been working as an employer in the State.
314: The appellant was a workman of the Indian National Bank and was employed as a workman. He was employed in the business of the appellant and was engaged in the work of the appellant. The appellant had been working as a clerk in the Indian Bank at the relevant time. The appellant did not pay any amount to the appellant but paid the same to the respondent. The appellant filed an application under section 123 Cr. P.C. before the High Court for quashing the order of discharge passed by the appellant on the ground that it was not a case of misappropriation or negligence. The High Court dismissed the petition holding that the order was not vitiated by mala fides and that the appellant was guilty of misconduct and misappropriation. Allowing the appeal to this Court, HELD: (1) The High Court's jurisdiction is not confined to the question whether the order made by the High court is justified or not. [68D] (2) The High Courts have no jurisdiction to entertain the complaint on the basis of the evidence adduced by the parties and the evidence led by the parties.
690: The assessee was a partner in the firm of the firm. The firm was a partnership firm and the partners were partners in the firm. In the assessment year 1951-52, the firm was assessed to tax under section 10 of the Income-tax Act, 1922 (hereinafter called the Act). The Income-tax Officer held that the firm had no business or business in the business. The High Court held that there was no business of the firm in which the firm carried on the business of manufacturing and selling the same as a partner and the firm did not carry on the business, and that the business was not an agent of the firm, but was an agent for the purpose of carrying on the business. Held, that the High Court was right in holding that the partnership was a firm and not a partner of the firm; that the partners of the partnership were not liable to be taxed under section 10(1) of the Act. The High Court, however, held that it was not necessary to refer to the decision of this Court in [Commissioner of Income-tax, Bombay v. M/s. Gordhandas Bhan] (1).
1789: The appellant was a workman of the Indian National Bank and was employed as a workman. The appellant had been working as a Manager in the Indian Bank at the relevant time on the basis of the contract between the appellant and the respondent and the appellant was engaged in the business of the appellant. The appellant filed an application under section 66(1) of the Act for the grant of leave to appeal against the order of the Industrial Tribunal and the Appellate Tribunal. The Tribunal by its judgment dated January 23, 1966 dismissed the application of the appellant holding that the appellant had not been paid the salary of the workmen of the respondent at the age of 55 years and that the workman was entitled to the benefit of the provisions of section 2(1)(a) of the Act. The appellant contended that the Tribunal had erred in law in holding that there was no provision in the Act or the rules made thereunder. The Tribunal held that the termination of the work done by the appellant is not a matter which is covered by the definition of the expression "workman" in section 2(2)(a). The Tribunal also held that it was not necessary to consider the question whether the termination was justified or not. Dismissing the appeal, HELD.
2122: The appellant was a member of the company and was a member. He was a partner in the company of the company. The appellant filed an application under section 237 of the Act for the grant of a certificate to the effect that he had no right to be appointed as a member or as a member, and that the appellant was not a member and was entitled to be appointed. The appellant contended that the agreement was not binding on the appellant. Held, that the High Court was right in holding that the contract was not valid because it was not enforceable by the provisions of the Act. [579A-B] (2) The High Court could not have interfered with the order of the Tribunal on the ground that the terms of the agreement were not binding upon the parties. N. Sachthey, for the appellants. M. C. Setalvad, Attorney-General for India, B. D. Sharma, A. K. Sen and P. L. Vohra, for the respondent.
2796: The appellants were convicted under section 376 I.P.C. and sentenced to imprisonment for life and a fine of Rs. 500/- each in default to suffer rigorous imprisonment for one year. The High Court held that the conviction was not justified. The High Court, however, upheld the conviction of the appellants. The High court has held that there was no evidence to show that the offence was committed by the appellants or that they had been acquitted by the trial court. The High Court's view is that the sentence of death imposed on the appellants, as already stated, was not a sufficient ground for convicting the appellants' conviction. The High Courts have also found that the appellant, who was the aggressor, was guilty of the offences under section 302 read with section 34 I.P. C., and sentenced him to undergo rigorous imprisonment of two years and to pay a fine thereof. The High Court. has come up in appeal against this judgment. The appellants-accused has challenged the conviction and sentence of the appellant under section 323 I.PC. The High court, however, has not considered the evidence adduced before it and has rejected the evidence of the prosecution witnesses and has held the appellant. The High court's judgment is based on the evidence which is not supported by any evidence.
6852: The appellants were convicted under Section 3 of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947 and sentenced to imprisonment for life and a fine of Rs. 500/- each in default to suffer rigorous imprisonment for one year and to pay a fine which was also imposed on them by the High Court. The sentences were directed to run concurrently. The appellants, however, filed an appeal against the judgment of the High Court of Punjab & Haryana at Chandigarh challenging the validity of the impugned order of conviction and sentence passed against them. The High Court dismissed the appeal holding that the appellants are not entitled to any compensation for the injuries sustained by them as they have been caused by the blunt object of the offending act and that the offence committed by them is not punishable under Section 4 of the Act. The High Court, therefore, set aside the conviction and sentence. The appellants' case is that the appellant has been convicted under Sections 3, 4 and 5 of the Act and sentenced him to undergo rigorous imprisonment under Section 7 of the Act, and he has been sentenced to undergo simple imprisonment for three years and to undergo further rigorous imprisonment of two years. The High court held that the conviction of the appellant's conviction under Section 6 of the Arms Act is unsustainable and the same is liable to be set aside.
2649: The firm was a partner in the partnership firm and the partners were partners of the firm. The firm had been registered as a partner under the Indian Income Tax Act, 1922. The firm filed an application for registration of the firm on the ground that the firm had not been registered under the Act and that the partnership was not a partnership firm and, therefore, the firm was liable to be assessed as a partner. The High Court held that the partners had no right to claim any share in the business of the firm, but the firm did not have any interest in the business. The High Court, however, held that there was no question of the partners being a partner or a partner of the firm; that the business was not carried on by the firm and that it was not liable to tax under the Act. Allowing the appeal to this Court, HELD: 1. The firm is a partnership firm, and the firm is not a partner within the meaning of section 2(9) of the Act. [953C-D] 2. The partnership firm is one of the partners. The partnership is a partner and the other is the partners of a firm. The partnership was dissolved on the basis of the partnership deed dated March 31, 1958. The partnership deed was executed on April 1, 1958 and the partnership had been dissolved on January.
6728: The appellants were the owners of the land in question and the lands in question were acquired by the appellants. They were the tenants of the appellants' land. The appellants, however, filed a writ petition before the High Court challenging the validity of the notification under section 4(1) of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894 (hereinafter referred to as 'the Act') on the ground that the acquisition was not for a public purpose and that the appellants had no right to be evicted from the land under the Act. The High Court dismissed the writ petition. The High Court, however, held that the provisions of the Act are applicable to the case of the respondents. The High Court's judgment is based on the decision of this Court in [State of Maharashtra v. M/s. R.K. Garg & Ors.] [AIR 1966 SC 1369]. In that case, the appellants, who were the respondents in the writ petition filed by them in the High Court, challenged the validity and validity of section 4(2) of the Act. On the other hand, the High court held that section 4(1)(c) of the Act, which was applicable to all the cases of the appellant was ultra vires and inoperative.
2052: The appellant company was a workman of the Indian Bank and was employed as a workman. The appellant was employed in the Indian Bank. The appellant filed an application under section 3 of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947 (hereinafter referred to as 'the Act') for making a reference to the Labour Court under section 34 of the Act. The Labour Court dismissed the application. The appellant preferred an appeal against the order of the Labour Court. The High Court held that the award of the tribunal was not a "workman" within the meaning of section 2(1)(a) of the Act and it was not liable to be set aside. The appellant challenged the order passed by the Labour Court, but the High Court allowed the appeal and set aside the order made by the Industrial Tribunal. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The appellant is a workman, who is engaged in the business of manufacturing and selling and selling the goods and is engaged by him in the manufacture of the same goods. [57F-G] 2. The appellant has been engaged in manufacturing and sale of the goods in the factory of the appellant. It is not a workman's case that the appellant had been engaged by the appellant in the production of the said goods and that he had been working in the factory.
5266: The appellant was a public trust and the appellant was an Indian company of which he was a private company. The appellant filed a suit against the appellant for a declaration that the appellant is a public trust. The trial court held that the appellant's suit was barred by limitation. The High Court dismissed the suit. The appellant preferred an appeal to this Court. The High Court, however, allowed the appeal and set aside the judgment of the trial court. The appellant contended that the suit was not maintainable as it had been filed in the court of the Subordinate Judge, First Class, Delhi, and that the trial court had no jurisdiction to entertain the suit on merits. The High Court's view was that the case was one of fact and the trial court, therefore, did not decide the question whether the appellant could be said to have committed any offence under Section 13(1)(a) of the Act. The High court also held that there was no evidence to show that the respondent was a 'public servant' within the meaning of Section 2(d). The High Courts were therefore right in holding that the finding of the High Court that the plaintiff was a "public servant" was not correct. In the result the appeal fails and is dismissed. The appellant is before us in this appeal. The appellant has come up in appeal by special leave.
5248: The assessee was a dealer under the Indian Income Tax Act and was a registered dealer under an Indian Income tax Act. The assessee claimed exemption from tax under section 13(1)(a) of the Act on the ground that it had not been paid in the course of its business and that the assessee had not paid any amount to the assessee. The assessee filed a writ petition before the High Court of Allahabad challenging the order of the Tribunal holding that the income of the assessee was not liable to be taxed under section 14(1) (b) of the Act. The High Court held that the question whether the assessee could have made a claim for deduction of income-tax under section 13 (2) (a) of that Act, was not raised before the Tribunal. The High Court, however, held that there was no question of law as to the interpretation of the relevant provisions of the Act, and the High Court's view was erroneous. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The High Court--is entitled to the benefit of section 13(1) (a) of Act XVI of 1956. [104 G] 2. The High Courts are not concerned with the question of law, but they are not dealing with the questions of law which are required to be decided by the High Court.
2304: The appellant was appointed as Assistant Commissioner of Police on the basis of a post of Deputy Secretary to the Government of India in the State of Bihar. He was promoted as Assistant Director of the State Police on April 1, 1966 and was confirmed on the same day. On March 31, 1966, he was promoted to the cadre of Assistant Commissioner (Judicial) with effect from January 1, 1966. The appellant filed an application under Article 226 of the Constitution before the High Court of Orissa for quashing the order of his removal from service dated September 30, 1967. The High Court dismissed the petition holding that the appellant is not a member of the Service and consequently the order passed by the High court is illegal and without jurisdiction. The High Court, however, held that the order made by the Government is illegal as it has been passed without jurisdiction and without jurisdiction and, therefore, the High Court's decision is unsustainable in law. The appeal is accordingly allowed. The judgment and order of the High Court, set aside and the writ petition filed by the appellant stands dismissed. No costs. PETITIONER: STATE OF PUNJAB Vs. RESPONDENT: THE STATE BANK OF INDIA & ORS.
6881: The appellant was a tenant of the appellant. He was a tenant, who was a member of the family of the appellant and was a partner in the said premises. The appellant filed an application under section 15(1)(d), of the R.P. Act for eviction of the respondent. The R.P.C. was dismissed by the Rent Controller on the ground that the appellant had not been a tenant within the meaning of section 15(1) (a). The Rent Control Tribunal held that the respondent was a landlord and not a tenant under the Re-Control Act. The Re-Controller allowed the application holding that the suit premises were not a tenant. The Rewa Court held that there was no evidence to show that the premises were let out to the appellant or that the Rewan Act did not apply to the case. The Rest Control Court held as under: "Section 15(1). Where a landlord is a tenant or a tenant in respect of any building or part of a building or a part of such building or portion thereof or part thereof, he shall be deemed to have been a tenant." The Rice Control Court also held that a tenant is a tenancy within the definition of the expression 'tenant' in section 2(1)(c).
6668: The plaintiff was a Hindu undivided family of the deceased and his son was married to one G.D. Seshiah on the basis of a compromise between the parties. The High Court held that the plaintiff was not a joint family property and the suit was barred by limitation. The High Court, however, held that there was no legal obligation on the part of the defendant to pay the amount due to him as a share in the property. The High court further held that it was not necessary for the plaintiff to prove that he had any interest in the property in the suit property. The trial court also held that since the plaintiff had no right to claim any interest therein and the plaintiff could not be said to have any interest therein. The High Court's judgment was affirmed by the High Court. The High Court. however, dismissed the appeal with costs which are to be paid to the plaintiff. The High Courts have concurrently found that the appellant is a Hindu family and has no right of pre-emption in respect of the property of the deceased. The High court, therefore, rightly set aside the decree passed by the trial court.
3531: NOTE: The appellant company was a workman of the Corporation and was employed as a workman. The workmen were employed by the appellant company in the year 1962. The workmen, who are the workmen of the Corporation, filed a writ petition before the High Court of Gujarat under Article 226 of the Constitution challenging the validity of the award on the ground that the workman had been appointed by the Board of Directors of the appellant. [576F] (3) The workman, who is the workman, has not been appointed as a Labour Officer or a workman, but has been appointed to the post of Assistant Manager of the Company. The appellant is a resident of the State of West Bengal and is a member of the Indian National Congress (I) and is engaged in the business of manufacturing and selling and selling goods and services essential to the community. 3019: The appellant was a member of the RANNAM and was a public servant of the State of Bihar. He was a government servant. The appellant filed an application under section 3(1) of the Army Act, 1954, for the grant of a writ in the nature of mandamus directing the appellant to pay a sum of Rs. 2,000/- as compensation for the unpaid amount of compensation. The appellant challenged the order of the High Court by filing a writ petition before the High Court. The High Court, on the other hand, held that the appellant had been a public servant, and that he was not a public servant; that the High Court, while dismissing the writ petition, did not consider it necessary to decide the question whether the appellant is a public servants or not. Allowing the appeal to this Court, HELD: 1. The appellant is an employee of the Central Government and is a Government servant. He is a government servant of a State and is not a Government servant of that State. [761F-G] 2. The appellant has been a Government servant's service and is an office of profit and loss of the Government. It is not necessary to go into the question of his being a Government servants. The appellant cannot be said to have been a government servant's service.
2248: The appellant was a Panchayat under the Bombay Municipal Act, 1925 and was a public servant of the State of West Bengal for the purpose of carrying on business in the State at the relevant time. The appellant filed an application under section 3 of the Act before the District Magistrate for the grant of a certificate under section 3(1) of the Act. The High Court dismissed the application. In appeal to this Court, HELD: 1. The provisions of the [Bombay Municipal Act] are not applicable to the present case. The High Court held that the levy of excise duty on goods manufactured and produced by the appellant is not a tax but a tax on the sale of the goods. The High Court, however, upheld the contention of the appellant that the goods are not covered by the provisions of section 4(4)(a) of the Act. The High Court's judgment was affirmed by this Court. In appeal to this Court it was contended that the appellant had not been able to prove that the value of the goods, which was sold by the appellants to the appellant as a result of the sale and the price of the imported goods was not a matter of fact and therefore the appellant could not be held liable for the same. 6413: The appellant was a public servant of the Indian Police and was employed as a public servant. He was a member of the Punjab Public Service Commission and was posted in the State of Punjab. The appellant contended that he was not a citizen of India and was not an employee of the Government. The High Court held that the appellant was not entitled to the benefit of section 302 of the Act. Allowing the appeal by special leave, HELD: 1. The appellant is a public servant; it is not a public servants but a public servants. It is not necessary to go into the question whether the appellant is an 'public servant' within the meaning of section 2(d)(b). [576C-D] 2. The appellant has been a public employee. 5471: The appellant was a tenant of the premises in question on the ground that he had been in occupation of the premises. The appellant filed an application under section 63(1) of the Act for eviction of the appellant from the premises on the grounds mentioned in the application. The High Court dismissed the petition holding that the appellant was not a tenant within the meaning of section 2(1)(a) of the Act. The High Court, however, held that the provisions of the Act, as amended by the Amendment Act of 1976, were applicable to the facts of the present case. The High Court's judgment is based on the interpretation of the relevant provisions of law and the High Court has held that it is not necessary to go into the merits of the case and decide the same on merits. [89C-D] JUDGMENT: CIVIL APPELLATE JURISDICTION: Civil Appeal No. 470 of 1988. From the Judgment and Order dated 13.2.1986 of the Bombay High Court in Writ Petition No. 75/87. V.P.S. Pathak, J. B. 3442: The appellant was a trustee of the appellant. He was a public trust and was a private trust. The appellant applied for a certificate of fitness to appeal to this Court on the ground that he had no right to claim the share of the property in the estate of the deceased and that he was entitled to receive the balance of the rent. The appellant contended that the appellant was not a public charitable trust, that the suit was barred by limitation. Held, that the High Court was right in holding that the respondent was a religious trust and that the property was a charitable trust and not a private trust and therefore the appellant could not be said to have been a public trust.
