362: The appellant was a dealer of the goods in the State of Bihar and was carrying on business in the State. The appellant claimed that he had been assessed to tax under section 4(1) of the Act as it stood at the relevant time and that the appellant was not liable to pay tax under the Act. The appellant contended that the levy of tax was illegal, and that there was no question of any interference by this Court in the appeal filed by the appellant. The High Court held that the imposition of tax on the appellant did not amount to an offence under section 302 of the Indian Penal Code and that it was not a case of sale or purchase of goods. The High Court, however, held that there were no grounds for holding that the impugned judgment and order of the High Court could not be sustained because the appellant had not made out a case for the levy and collection of tax under s. 4(1). Allowing the appeal, HELD: 1. The appellant is a dealer in the course of its business and is a dealer. He has not been charged with the commission of an offence punishable under section 3(1) of that Act.
2035: The workmen were employed by the Central Government in the year 1956. They were employed on a contract basis and were employed as a workman under the provisions of the Act. The workmen, who are the workmen of the company were not entitled to any relief. The workman was entitled to the benefit of the provisions contained in the Act and the rules framed thereunder. The workmen's claim for compensation was rejected by the Labour Court and the award was confirmed by the High Court. The Labour Court held that the workman had no right to claim the benefit under the Act or the Rules framed thereunder and that the employer was entitled only to the benefits of the Act as well as the provisions relating to the conditions of service of the workman. The Labour Court, however, held that there was no provision in the Act, which provided that the employee's right to receive compensation should be exercised by the employer and that it was not a right to recover the amount due from him under the Act. Allowing the appeal to this Court, HELD: (1) The Industrial Tribunal has jurisdiction to decide the question whether the workman, who is employed by an employer under the [Industrial Disputes Act] is a workman; and if so, what is the effect of the definition of the expression "workman" in the Act.
5597: The appellant was a tenant of the premises in occupation of the respondent. The appellant filed an application under Section 8 of the Act for eviction of the tenant on the ground that the premises were not let out to him and he had no right to be evicted from the premises. The Rent Controller dismissed the application. The appellant preferred an appeal against the order of the Rent Controller. The Appellate Authority allowed the appeal and set aside the order passed by the Rent-Controller and directed the landlord to vacate the premises within six months from the date of the order. The Appellate Authority, however, held that the appellant was not a tenant and the tenant was not entitled to evict the tenant from the premises as a tenant. The Appellate Court held that there was no evidence to show that the tenant had any right to evict. The Appellate Tribunal held that it was not necessary to prove that the landlord was a member of the tenant's family and that the rent was paid by the landlord for the period of three years from the commencement of the Act. The Appellate Bench held that since the tenant is a tenant under the Rent, the tenant must be deemed to have been a tenant at the time of the commencement and the rent should be paid by him.
2256: The appellant was a tenant of the premises in question on the ground that he had not been evicted from the premises. The appellant filed an application under section 17(1)(a) of the Act for eviction of the appellant on the grounds mentioned in the plaint. The appellant contended that the appellant was not entitled to claim the benefit of section 4 of the Act. The High Court dismissed the application. Allowing the appeal by special leave, HELD: (1) The appellant is a tenant under the Bombay Tenancy Act, 1949, and the appellant is entitled to the benefit under section 4(2) of the Act, if he is not a tenant within the meaning of section 2(l) of the Act; and it is not necessary to go into this question as we have already indicated. [106] (b) The appellant has no right to claim any benefit under the decree under section 23(1)(a). [107B-C] (c) The appellant cannot be said to have been evicted. [108D-E] (c) In the present case, the appellant has not been able to establish that the respondent was a tenant. The appellant could not have been given a right to get the benefit which he had to pay under the decree.
5861: The appellant was a member of the Indian Administrative Service and was appointed as a Member of the State Legislature. The appellant filed an application under section 3(1) of the Act for appointment of a Member to the Government of India in the Ministry of Home Affairs on the basis of the recommendation made by the Central Government. The appellant challenged the validity of the said order before the High Court of Judicature at Allahabad in Writ Petition No. 4211 of 1986. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the appellant had been appointed as the President of the Union Territory of Chandigarh and that he was not a member thereof. The High Court, however, held that the post of the President was not an office of profit and therefore the appellant could not be appointed as an Assistant Secretary to the Government, but was also entitled to be appointed to the post in question. The High court held that there was no question of the appellant being a member or a member who is not a Member and that the appointment of the respondent was not valid. Allowing the appeal to this Court, HELD: 1. The appellant is a member and has been appointed to a post in the State of Bihar and is a member. He is a person who is a Member in the State. The appointment of an Assistant Director is a part of the cadre of the State.
4480: The appellant was a dealer of the Union of India and was a partner in the State of Andhra Pradesh. The respondent filed an application under section 49(3) of the Act for recovery of possession of the property from the appellant. The High Court dismissed the application. In appeal to this Court, HELD: 1. The appellant is a company incorporated under the Companies Act, 1956 and is a registered dealer under the [Companies Act] and is not a registered dealer. The appellant has been carrying on business as a dealer under a registered trade name and is engaged in the business of manufacturing and selling the same in the State. The appellant had no right to carry on the business as such but it was not a dealer within the meaning of the Act. [857F-G] 2. The appellant cannot be said to have purchased the property in the name of the appellant from the State Government or from the Central Government. The appellant could not be said that he was a registered firm under the provisions of the [Societies Registration Act, 1860]. The appellant did not acquire any right to purchase the property by way of sale of the property. The appellant claimed that he had purchased the land from the appellant and that he would be entitled to purchase it.
784: The appellant was a tenant of the respondent No. 1 in respect of the lease. The respondent No. 2 had been paying rent for the period from April 1, 1944 to March 31, 1944, and the lease was for a period of three years from the date of the agreement which was the date on which the lease came into force. The respondent No.1 was a lessee of the premises in question and was not a party to the agreement. The respondent filed an application under s. 11 of the Act for the grant of a lease of the premises. The respondent contended that the lease had been terminated by the respondent on January 26, 1955, and that the respondent had no right to continue in possession of the property as it was a part of the lease and therefore the respondent was entitled to the benefit of the provisions of the Act. The High Court held that the terms of the deed were not binding on the parties and that there was no reason why the lease should be deemed to have been terminated without the consent of the parties. The High Court, however, held that there is no substance in this contention.
